1.sense: The surah begins with an order to speak and then supplies the words. What follows is not the Prophet ﷺ's own position being explained; it is a message handed to him to read out to people standing in front of him.

notes.t: Kafara means to cover something over. Classical Arabic calls the farmer who buries seed a kafir of the seed, and calls the night a kafir because it covers the day. Disbelief in the Qur'an's vocabulary is covering something that has already been shown.

The address is definite, al-kafirun, and the exegetes read it as aimed at a specific group of Quraysh who had put a proposal to the Prophet ﷺ, not as a form of address to every non-Muslim in every era.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the address as directed at named individuals of Quraysh

notes.t: Five surahs of the Qur'an open on the command Say. Four of them are short declarations of creed or refuge, and this is the one that draws a line between two parties.

links.why: the other short surah opening on Say, and the one paired with it in practice
Say, I am forbidden to worship those you call on besides Allah

2.sense: The first denial, in the present tense. I do not worship what you worship. It refuses the object rather than the act; both parties worship, and the whole difference is in what.

notes.t: The Arabic is maa, what, rather than man, whom. The objects of their worship are referred to with the pronoun used for things. The choice is not neutral and would have been heard.
The verb rather than a noun. He does not say I am not one of your religion, which would be a statement about membership. He says I do not do that, which is a statement about practice.

The Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah together with al-Ikhlas in the two units before the dawn prayer, so that the two shortest statements of what is worshipped and what is not were said at the start of every day.
notes.src: Muslim, Book of the Prayer of Travellers, on the two rakʿahs of Fajr, from Abu Hurayra

links.why: Say, if you are in doubt about my religion, I do not worship what you worship besides Allah
Say, is it other than Allah you order me to worship

3.sense: The mirror image, and the grammar shifts. Where the last verse used a verb of him, this one uses a noun of them. Not you do not worship, but you are not worshippers, which describes a standing condition rather than a current act.

notes.t: ʿAabidoon is an active participle, and Arabic participles state a settled description. The line is not reporting what they failed to do this morning; it is saying what kind of party they are with respect to this object.
The same neutral word maa is used for the true object of worship as for theirs, which keeps the two halves of the sentence exactly parallel and makes the whole weight fall on who is worshipping what.

Nothing in the surah insults their gods by name. The Qur'an elsewhere forbids abusing what other people call on, lest they abuse Allah in ignorance, and this surah observes that restraint while refusing everything.

links.why: do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, so they do not insult Allah in enmity
Ibrahim asking his people, have you seen what you have been worshipping

4.sense: The third denial, and now the tense moves. What you have worshipped, in the past. The line closes off any suggestion that he ever had a share in it before the message came.

notes.t: ʿAbadtum is past tense, and it is the one clear change of tense in the four denials. Verse two ruled out the present; this rules out the record. There is no earlier period being appealed to.

The exegetes who studied the repetition read verses two and three as covering the present and verses four and five as covering the past and what will follow. Others read the second pair as emphasis alone, which is ordinary Arabic practice.
notes.src: az-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir set out both explanations

notes.t: The Qur'an gives the same refusal in a longer form elsewhere, telling the Prophet ﷺ to say that his prayer, his rites, his living and his dying belong to the Lord of the worlds.

links.why: my prayer, my rites, my living and my dying are for the Lord of the worlds
you are clear of what I do and I am clear of what you do

5.sense: The line from verse three comes back word for word. Nothing is added and nothing is softened. The repetition is the door being shut a second time on the same hinge.

notes.t: Exact repetition inside a surah is not unusual in the Qur'an; Surah ar-Rahman repeats one verse thirty-one times. What is unusual here is that the repeated line is a refusal, and that it comes back after only one intervening verse.

Many grammarians read the second occurrence as carrying a future sense, nor will you ever be, which completes the coverage of past, present and future across the four denials. Others hold that it is emphasis and nothing more.
notes.src: the exegetes differ; at-Tabari reports the emphasis reading and later commentators develop the tense reading

notes.t: The surah spends four of its six verses saying the same thing from two sides. The design refuses the middle position it is answering, which was an offer to share worship in alternate years.

links.why: the Qur'an's other worked case of a line repeated deliberately
it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them

6.sense: The settlement, in four words with no verb in it. Two parties, two religions, and no shared one. The verse states a separation rather than granting a permission.

notes.t: This is not indifference about truth. Five verses have just refused to merge the two practices, and this line says what is left after the refusal, which is that each party keeps its own and neither performs the other's.

Some held that the verse was abrogated by the later verses of fighting. Many exegetes rejected this, on the ground that it reports a fact about who worships what rather than issuing a ruling that could be replaced.
notes.src: the claim of abrogation is recorded and rejected by Ibn Kathir among others

notes.t: The final word is written diin without its yaa, matching the rhyme of the surah. The Mushaf's spelling follows the recitation here rather than the ordinary grammar of the possessive.

links.why: there is no compulsion in religion, the ruling that matches this statement
the same separation stated as a formula of disavowal
